title: Caching
summary: Where caches live, how to read and write through them, eviction, invalidation, HTTP caching, distributed caches and the failure modes that take systems down.

lessons.title: Why cache, and where
lessons.summary: What a cache buys you, the layers it can live in from browser to buffer pool, and the hit-ratio maths that tells you whether it is working.
lessons.body:
A **cache** is a small, fast store that keeps copies of data that lives somewhere slower or more expensive. You put one in front of a source of truth so that repeated requests for the same thing don't pay the full cost every time.

Caching helps when a workload has reuse or skew. Some workloads approximate a Zipf-like popularity pattern, but a fixed 80/20 split is not universal; measure the actual access distribution. In workloads with temporal locality, a value read once is likely to be read again soon. This is called **locality of reference**: *temporal* locality (the same item again) and *spatial* locality (nearby items).

## What a cache buys you

There are three separate benefits, and it helps to know which one you are after.

- **Lower latency.** A local memory lookup can avoid network and backend work. Exact latency depends on hardware, software, payload and load; universal nanosecond/millisecond benchmarks are absent because no matched measurements are supplied.
- **Less load on the backend.** Every hit is a request your database never sees. A 95% hit ratio means the database handles 1 in 20 reads.
- **Lower cost.** Serving bytes from a CDN edge or from RAM is often far cheaper than recomputing a page or paying for database capacity.

The price you pay is **staleness** and **complexity**. A cache holds a copy, and copies can disagree with the original. Most of this module is about managing that cost.

> [!note] A cache is not a database
> Treat cached data as disposable. If the cache is wiped, the system should get slower, not wrong. If losing the cache loses data, you have built a database without a database's guarantees.

## The layers where caches live

A single web request can pass through half a dozen caches before it reaches the disk.

```
 Browser cache     (per user, HTTP headers)
      |
 CDN edge          (shared, near the user)
      |
 Reverse proxy     (Varnish / Nginx)
      |
 App server        (in-process memory)
      |
 Distributed cache (Redis / Memcached)
      |
 Database          (buffer pool, page cache)
      |
 Disk
```

Each layer sits closer to the user than the one below it. Caching closer to the user saves more latency but gives you less control over invalidation.

| Layer | Main saving | Who controls it |
|---|---|---|
| Browser | Network request | Browser and response policy |
| CDN edge | Origin trip | Provider configuration |
| Reverse proxy | Application work | Service operator |
| In-process | Network and decoding work | Application |
| Redis / Memcached | Database work | Cache operator |
| DB buffer pool | Storage reads | Database |

### Browser cache

The browser stores responses keyed by URL and obeys `Cache-Control`, `ETag` and friends. It is local to a browser profile, not necessarily one application account. A long freshness lifetime permits reuse; it does not guarantee retention. Supporting browsers can honor Clear-Site-Data on a later response, but there is no universal immediate remote purge of every browser. That is why static assets use **fingerprinted file names** such as `app.3f9a1c.js`. A new version is a new URL, so the old cached copy simply stops being requested.

### CDN edge

A CDN keeps copies in hundreds of points of presence (PoPs) worldwide, so a user in Sydney fetches from Sydney rather than from Virginia. It is a **shared** cache, so it must never store one user's private response and hand it to another. CDNs are covered in the networking module; here, remember that they are just another HTTP cache with a purge API.

### Reverse proxy

Varnish, Nginx (`proxy_cache`) or a cloud load balancer can cache full HTTP responses in front of your app servers. This is very effective for pages that are the same for every anonymous visitor, such as a news homepage.

### Application cache

This is the cache you code against. There are two flavours:

- **In-process** (a dictionary, Caffeine in Java, `functools.lru_cache` in Python). Fastest possible, with no network hop and no serialisation. But each server has its own copy, so 50 servers means 50 copies that can disagree, and memory is limited to one process.
- **Remote / distributed** (Redis, Memcached). A shared service (possibly with multiple replicas), accessed over the network at deployment-dependent latency. Survives app deploys and scales independently.

Many systems use both: a tiny in-process cache with a short TTL (say 1–5 seconds) in front of Redis, to absorb very hot keys.

### Database buffer pool

Databases cache too. PostgreSQL keeps recently used 8 KB pages in `shared_buffers` and also relies on the operating system's page cache. PostgreSQL's docs suggest starting `shared_buffers` at about 25% of RAM on a dedicated server. MySQL's InnoDB has the **buffer pool**, which on a dedicated host is often given up to about 80% of RAM. Cached pages avoid storage reads, but the speedup depends on query execution, hardware and the rest of the workload.

> [!tip] The "free" cache
> Before adding Redis, check that your database's working set fits in RAM. Sizing the buffer pool correctly is often the cheapest caching win available.

## Hit ratio maths

The **hit ratio** `h` is the fraction of lookups served from the cache:

```
h = hits / (hits + misses)
```

The **average access time** is a weighted sum. On a miss you usually pay the cache lookup *and* the backend:

```
T_avg = T_cache + (1 - h) * T_backend
```

### A worked example

Redis takes 1 ms; the database takes 20 ms.

| Hit ratio | Average latency | DB reads per 10k |
|---|---|---|
| No cache lookup | 20 ms | 10,000 |
| 0% (cache checked) | 21 ms | 10,000 |
| 80% | 1 + 0.2×20 = 5 ms | 2,000 |
| 90% | 1 + 0.1×20 = 3 ms | 1,000 |
| 99% | 1 + 0.01×20 = 1.2 ms | 100 |

Notice what happens between 90% and 99%. Latency only falls from 3 ms to 1.2 ms, but **database load falls tenfold**, from 1,000 to 100 reads. The useful number is often the **miss ratio** `(1 - h)`, because that is what your backend actually sees. Going from 99% to 99.9% barely registers on a latency chart (1.2 ms to 1.02 ms), but it cuts backend load by another 10×.

This is also why losing a cache is so dangerous. If the database is sized for a 1% miss rate and the cache disappears, it suddenly receives 100× its usual traffic. Lesson 7 covers this failure mode.

### Stacked caches

When caches sit in layers, each one only sees the misses of the layer above. Suppose an in-process cache catches 50% of reads and Redis catches 90% of what is left:

```
DB share = (1 - 0.5) * (1 - 0.9)
         = 0.5 * 0.1 = 0.05
```

Together they achieve a 95% hit ratio. Notice that Redis's *own* hit ratio looks lower than it would without the in-process layer, because the in-process cache has already taken the easiest, hottest keys. Judge each layer by what it saves the layer below, not by its ratio in isolation.

### Is caching worth it here?

A cache helps when:

1. Reads greatly outnumber writes for the same key.
2. The same keys are requested repeatedly (skewed access).
3. Slightly stale data is acceptable, or you can invalidate reliably.
4. The value is expensive to produce: a slow query, an aggregation, a rendered page, a remote API call.

A cache helps little or hurts when every request is for a different key (a long-tail scan), when data changes on almost every read, or when correctness requires the very latest value (a bank balance used to authorise a payment).

> [!warning] Misses can cost more than no cache
> A miss pays the cache round trip *plus* the backend. If your hit ratio is very low, you have added latency and a new failure point for almost no benefit.

## Sizing: how big should it be?

You rarely need to cache everything. Because access is skewed, the required fraction of cached keys depends on the observed popularity distribution. The usual approach is:

1. Estimate the **working set**: the distinct keys touched in a typical window (an hour or a day).
2. Multiply by average value size plus overhead (measure key, value, allocator and metadata overhead with representative objects; no fixed per-key overhead applies universally).
3. Measure the hit ratio at a few sizes. The curve of hit ratio against cache size flattens out; stop where extra memory stops buying meaningful hits.

For example, 5 million active users with a 2 KB profile is about 10 GB of values plus ~0.5 GB of overhead, under an illustrative 100-byte-overhead assumption. This is payload sizing, not a node recommendation; add measured fragmentation, buffers, replication and snapshot headroom.

## Key takeaways
- Caches work because access is skewed and repeated (locality of reference).
- They cut latency, backend load and cost, at the price of staleness and complexity.
- Caches exist at every layer: browser, CDN, reverse proxy, in-process, distributed, and inside the database.
- `T_avg = T_cache + (1 - h) × T_backend`. Watch the **miss ratio**: it is what your backend sees.
- Moving from 90% to 99% hit ratio cuts backend load by 10×, so losing the cache can overwhelm the database.
- Cached data must be disposable: losing it should make things slower, never wrong.

## Further reading
- [Cache (computing) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cache_(computing))
- [Caching overview — AWS](https://aws.amazon.com/caching/)
- [Latency numbers every programmer should know](https://gist.github.com/jboner/2841832)
- [PostgreSQL resource consumption (shared_buffers)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html)
- [Locality of reference — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locality_of_reference)

questions.prompt: Why does a cache that holds only 10% of all keys often achieve a hit ratio well above 10%?

options.text: Because caches compress data, so 10% of the memory holds far more than 10% of the keys
options.explanation: Compression may help memory use, but the premise says the cache holds 10% of the keys. The hit ratio is about which keys are requested, not how they are stored.

options.text: Because every miss automatically loads all neighbouring keys into the cache
options.explanation: Pre-fetching neighbours (spatial locality) is used in CPU caches and some databases, but it is not an automatic property of application caches and does not explain the general effect.

options.text: Because the hit ratio counts writes as hits
options.explanation: Hit ratio is defined over lookups: hits divided by hits plus misses. Writes are not counted as hits.

options.text: Because real access patterns are skewed: a small set of popular keys receives most requests
options.explanation: Correct. Many cache-friendly workloads exhibit skew, but it must be measured, and requests repeat over time (temporal locality). If the cache holds the hottest 10% of keys, those may account for 80–95% of lookups.

questions.workedExample:
1. Hit ratio depends on **which keys are asked for**, not how many keys exist.
2. Suppose 1 million products, and the top 100,000 (10%) receive 90% of page views, as an explicit hypothetical distribution, not a universal e-commerce measurement.
3. If the cache holds those 100,000 products, then 90% of lookups find their key: `h ≈ 0.9`.
4. The remaining 900,000 products share the other 10% of traffic, so caching them adds little.
5. So skew (popularity) plus repetition (temporal locality) is what makes small caches effective.

questions.prompt: Redis responds in 1 ms and your database in 20 ms. On a miss, the app checks Redis first, then queries the database. What is the average read latency at an 85% hit ratio?

options.text: 1 ms
options.explanation: That would only be true at a 100% hit ratio. 15% of requests still go to the database.

options.text: 4 ms
options.explanation: Correct. Every request pays the 1 ms cache lookup, and the 15% that miss also pay 20 ms: `1 + 0.15 × 20 = 4 ms`.
Close, but this uses `0.85 × 1 + 0.15 × 20 = 3.85`, which forgets that misses also pay the 1 ms cache lookup before going to the database.

options.text: 17 ms
options.explanation: This is `0.85 × 20`, which weights the database by the hit ratio instead of the miss ratio. Hits are the requests that avoid the database.

questions.workedExample:
Use `T_avg = T_cache + (1 - h) × T_backend`.

1. `T_cache = 1 ms` is paid on **every** request, hit or miss, because you always look in the cache first.
2. Miss ratio `= 1 - 0.85 = 0.15`.
3. Backend cost on misses `= 0.15 × 20 = 3 ms`.
4. Total `= 1 + 3 = 4 ms`.

Compare with no cache: 20 ms. The cache gives a 5× speed-up and cuts database reads by 85%.

questions.prompt: Your cache hit ratio rises from 99% to 99.9% after you double the cache size. Latency barely moves on the dashboard. What is the most important effect of this change?

options.text: Nothing significant: a 0.9 percentage point gain is noise
options.explanation: This judges the change by the hit ratio, but the backend experiences the miss ratio, which has fallen from 1% to 0.1%, a 10× change.

options.text: Average latency falls by 10×
options.explanation: Average latency is dominated by the cache lookup once the hit ratio is high. With 1 ms cache and 20 ms DB, it goes from 1.2 ms to 1.02 ms, about 15%, not 10×.

options.text: Database read load falls by roughly 10×
options.explanation: Correct. Misses fall from 1 in 100 to 1 in 1,000 requests. At 100k req/s, database reads drop from 1,000/s to 100/s, which frees capacity and reduces tail latency under load.

options.text: The cache now needs less memory per key
options.explanation: Hit ratio has nothing to do with per-key memory. Doubling the cache used more memory in total.

questions.workedExample:
1. Assume 100,000 reads/s, cache 1 ms, DB 20 ms.
2. At 99%: misses `= 1% × 100,000 = 1,000/s`. Latency `= 1 + 0.01 × 20 = 1.2 ms`.
3. At 99.9%: misses `= 0.1% × 100,000 = 100/s`. Latency `= 1 + 0.001 × 20 = 1.02 ms`.
4. Latency improved ~15%. **Database load improved 10×.**
5. Lesson: once hit ratios are high, think in miss ratios. That is the number that decides how big your database must be.

questions.prompt: Assume short-lived staleness is acceptable for displayed product prices, FX quotes and anonymous pages; payment authorization still requires authoritative transactional checks. Which of these workloads are **good** candidates for adding a cache? Select all that apply.

options.text: A product page read 50,000 times for every price update
options.explanation: Correct. A huge read-to-write ratio on the same key means each cached copy serves many reads before it needs refreshing.

options.text: A nightly job that scans every row of a 2 TB table exactly once
options.explanation: Not a good fit. Each row is read once, so there is no reuse. Caching it would just churn memory and evict useful data (this is called cache pollution).

options.text: A slow third-party exchange-rate API whose values change every few minutes
options.explanation: Correct. The call is expensive and slow, many requests share the same answer, and a staleness of a minute or so is acceptable. A short TTL fits well.

options.text: The account balance check that authorises a card payment
options.explanation: Not a good fit. Authorisation needs the latest committed balance. A stale cached value could approve a payment that overdraws the account.

options.text: A rendered homepage that is identical for all anonymous visitors
options.explanation: Correct. One copy serves everyone, it is expensive to render, and it can be cached at the reverse proxy or CDN for seconds to minutes.

questions.workedExample:
Check each workload against four tests:

1. **Read-heavy?** 2. **Repeated keys?** 3. **Staleness acceptable?** 4. **Expensive to produce?**

| Workload | Reuse | Stale OK | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Product page | Very high | Seconds | Cache |
| Full table scan | None | n/a | Don't |
| FX rate API | High | Minutes | Cache |
| Balance for auth | High | No | Don't |
| Anonymous homepage | Very high | Seconds | Cache |

The scan fails on reuse; the balance check fails on staleness.

questions.prompt: You run 40 app servers, each with an in-process cache of user profiles (TTL 10 minutes). Assume no stale in-flight refill or replica lag, and no invalidation on writes. A user changes their display name. What will they most likely experience?

options.text: The name flips between old and new on refresh, depending on which server the load balancer picks, for up to 10 minutes
options.explanation: Correct. Each server has its own copy. Servers that cached the old name keep serving it until their entry expires, so requests landing on different servers see different values.

options.text: The new name appears everywhere immediately, because the database was updated
options.explanation: The database is updated, but 40 independent in-process caches still hold the old value until their TTL expires or they are explicitly invalidated.

options.text: The old name appears for exactly 10 minutes on every server, then changes everywhere at once
options.explanation: Each server cached the profile at a different time, so each entry expires at a different moment. There is no single synchronised switch-over.

options.text: The update fails, because in-process caches lock the row
options.explanation: In-process caches hold copies; they do not take database locks. The write succeeds.

questions.workedExample:
1. In-process means **one cache per server**: 40 separate copies.
2. Server A cached the profile at 10:00, server B at 10:07, server C never cached it.
3. The user renames at 10:08.
4. A request to C misses and reads the new name. A request to A shows the old name until 10:10. B shows it until 10:17.
5. The load balancer spreads requests, so the user sees the name flicker.

Fixes: use a shared cache with reliable invalidation (Redis alone does not ensure freshness), shorten the in-process TTL to a few seconds, or broadcast invalidations (for example via Redis pub/sub).

questions.prompt: Your database can sustain 5,000 reads/s. Peak traffic is 200,000 reads/s and the cache hit ratio is 98%. A bad deploy flushes the cache. Roughly what happens, and what does it tell you about capacity planning?

options.text: The database sees about 4,000 reads/s before and after, because the hit ratio is a property of the workload
options.explanation: Hit ratio depends on what the cache currently holds. An empty cache has a hit ratio near 0%, so almost every request goes to the database.

options.text: Load rises to 10,000/s, double the normal miss rate
options.explanation: This underestimates badly. A flushed cache does not merely double misses; it turns almost every request into a miss until it warms up.

options.text: Nothing changes for the database; the app servers just get slower
options.explanation: The app servers get slower because they are waiting on the database, which is now receiving almost all traffic.

options.text: The database load jumps from about 4,000/s to nearly 200,000/s, 40× its capacity, so it falls over unless traffic is shed or the cache refills quickly
options.explanation: Correct. Normal misses are `2% × 200,000 = 4,000/s`, within capacity. With an empty cache, nearly all 200,000/s miss. The database was only ever sized for the miss traffic, so the cache is effectively a load-bearing part of the system.

questions.workedExample:
1. Normal DB load `= (1 - 0.98) × 200,000 = 4,000 reads/s`, under the 5,000/s limit.
2. After a flush, the hit ratio is ~0%, so DB load `≈ 200,000 reads/s`.
3. `200,000 / 5,000 = 40×` overload. Queries queue, latency soars, connections are exhausted, and the cache cannot refill because the database is too slow to answer.
4. Capacity-planning lesson: if the backend cannot survive the cache disappearing, the cache is **critical infrastructure**. Plan for it with replicas, warming, request coalescing, rate-limiting misses, and load shedding (covered in lesson 7).

questions.prompt: Why do sites serve JavaScript bundles with fingerprinted names like `app.3f9a1c.js` and a one-year cache lifetime?

options.text: Because browsers refuse to cache files without a hash in the name
options.explanation: Browsers cache any response permitted by its headers; the file name does not matter to the browser.

options.text: Changing content produces a new URL, so updated HTML requests the new asset without waiting for old cached entries to expire.
options.explanation: Correct. Fingerprinting avoids dependence on remotely clearing every browser. Long freshness does not guarantee cache retention or a perfect hit ratio.

options.text: Because the hash encrypts the file so CDNs cannot read it
options.explanation: The hash is a content fingerprint in the URL, not encryption. The CDN reads and serves the file normally.

options.text: Because it makes the file smaller
options.explanation: Adding a hash to the name has no effect on file size.

questions.workedExample:
1. A browser may reuse a fresh response without contacting the site.
2. Content-hashed asset URLs change when their bytes change.
3. Updated HTML refers to the new URL, which can be fetched independently of the old cached asset.
4. Clear-Site-Data can request cache clearing in supporting browsers once a response reaches them, but it is not a universal instant remote purge.
5. Eviction, user settings and stale HTML still affect cache hits and update visibility.

questions.prompt: Each app server has an in-process cache that serves 60% of reads. Behind it, Redis serves 75% of the reads that reach it. What fraction of all reads reach the database?

options.explanation: This is Redis's own miss ratio, but Redis only sees the 40% of reads the in-process layer missed.
This subtracts the miss ratios (40% − 25%) instead of multiplying them. Each layer filters what the layer above let through.
Correct. `(1 − 0.6) × (1 − 0.75) = 0.4 × 0.25 = 0.10`, so the combined hit ratio is 90%.
This is the in-process miss ratio. It ignores the reads that Redis then catches.

questions.workedExample:
1. Start with 100 reads.
2. In-process hits 60, so **40** go to Redis.
3. Redis hits 75% of 40 = 30, so **10** go to the database.
4. Database share `= 10 / 100 = 10%`.

General rule for stacked caches:

```
DB = (1 - h1) * (1 - h2)
```

Redis's 75% looks mediocre, but that is because the in-process layer already took the hottest keys.

questions.prompt: You have 20 million registered users, of whom 4 million are active in a typical day. Each cached session object is about 1.5 KB, and Assume measurements for this exact deployment show 80 bytes of overhead per key. Roughly how much memory should you plan for the daily working set?

options.text: About 6.3 GB
options.explanation: Correct. `4M × (1,500 + 80) B ≈ 6.3 GB`. Size for the working set, then add headroom for fragmentation and growth.

options.text: About 31.6 GB
options.explanation: This sizes for all 20 million registered users. Users who are not active today mostly won't be in the cache, and caching them buys few hits.

options.text: About 6.0 GB
options.explanation: This counts the values but forgets per-key overhead, which is about 5% here and much more for small values.

options.text: About 320 MB
options.explanation: This counts only the per-key overhead (`4M × 80 B`) and leaves out the values themselves.

questions.workedExample:
1. Working set = distinct keys touched in the window = **4 million** active users, not 20 million registered.
2. Bytes per key `= 1,500 + 80 = 1,580 B`.
3. Total:

```
4,000,000 * 1,580 B
= 6.32e9 B ≈ 6.3 GB
```

4. Add headroom (say 25–50%) for fragmentation, replication buffers and growth, so plan for an 8–10 GB node.
5. Then measure the hit ratio at a few sizes: skew may mean a smaller cache gets almost the same hits.

questions.prompt: You are choosing between an in-process cache and a shared Redis cache for product data on 30 app servers. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: An in-process lookup avoids a network round trip and can reduce latency.
options.explanation: Correct. The actual cost depends on language, data structure, serialization and workload; there is no universal 100 ns application lookup guarantee.

options.text: With one coalesced cold fill per server, up to 30 independent servers may load the same key.
options.explanation: Correct under that assumption. Without per-process coalescing, concurrent misses can produce more than one load per server.

options.text: A Redis cache is lost whenever an app server is redeployed
options.explanation: Incorrect. Redis runs as a separate service, so it survives app deploys. It is the in-process cache that is emptied on every restart.

options.text: An in-process cache keeps all 30 servers consistent with each other automatically
options.explanation: Incorrect. Each server holds an independent copy, so they can disagree until each entry expires or is invalidated.

options.text: A small in-process cache with a 1–5 s TTL in front of Redis can absorb very hot keys
options.explanation: Correct when short local staleness is acceptable. Local TTL bounds time since insertion, not total age inherited from Redis or a lagging source.

questions.workedExample:
1. Local caches avoid the network but each process has its own contents.
2. Shared Redis centralizes access, but replicas, invalidation races and stale origin data still affect consistency with the database.
3. A separate Redis service survives app restarts; a process-local cache does not.
4. Combining tiers can reduce hot-key load; measure latency and include every layer when setting freshness objectives.

questions.prompt: Every request checks Redis (1 ms) before querying a 10 ms database. Below what hit ratio does the cache make *average* latency worse than having no cache at all?

options.explanation: At 50%, `1 + 0.5 × 10 = 6 ms`, which is still better than 10 ms with no cache.
At 1%, `1 + 0.99 × 10 = 10.9 ms`, which is already worse than 10 ms. The break-even point is higher than this.
At 90% the average is `1 + 0.1 × 10 = 2 ms`, a large improvement. The break-even is far lower.
Correct. Solve `1 + (1 − h) × 10 = 10`, giving `h = 0.1`. Below a 10% hit ratio the cache costs more latency than it saves.

questions.workedExample:
1. With the cache: `T = 1 + (1 - h) × 10`.
2. Without it: `T = 10`.
3. Break-even:

```
1 + (1 - h) * 10 = 10
(1 - h) * 10 = 9
h = 0.1
```

4. In general, break-even `h = T_cache / T_backend`.
5. Latency is not the only consideration: even at a low hit ratio the cache may still shed useful load. But you have also added a new dependency that can fail.

questions.prompt: A team stores shopping baskets *only* in Redis, with no persistence and no copy in the database, because "it is just a cache and it's fast". A Redis node is restarted during a deploy. What is the core design mistake?

options.text: They should have used Memcached, which keeps data across restarts
options.explanation: Memcached is purely in-memory too. Swapping products doesn't fix the fact that the data has no durable home.

options.text: Redis was being used as the system of record, so losing the cache lost data instead of just making things slower
options.explanation: Correct. Cached data must be disposable. Baskets that exist nowhere else are not a cache entry; they are primary data that needs a durable store (or Redis configured and operated as a database).

options.text: The TTL on the baskets was too long
options.explanation: TTL controls staleness, not durability. Any TTL would still lose the baskets on restart.

options.text: The hit ratio was too low
options.explanation: Hit ratio is irrelevant here. The problem is that there was nothing to fall back to on a miss.

questions.workedExample:
1. Apply the lesson's test: *if the cache is wiped, does the system get slower or wrong?*
2. Here, a wipe means customers' baskets vanish. That is **wrong**, not slower.
3. So Redis was acting as a database without a database's durability guarantees.
4. Fixes: write baskets to a durable store and cache them in front, or deliberately run Redis as a primary store (persistence, replication, backups) and treat it with database-level care.

lessons.title: Caching strategies
lessons.summary: Cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-back and write-around — how data flows between app, cache and database, and what each costs.
lessons.body:
Once you have decided to cache, you have to decide **who loads the cache, and what happens on a write**. These choices are called caching strategies (or patterns). They differ in who is responsible for the cache, how fresh the data is, and what can be lost when something crashes.

Read strategies decide how data gets *into* the cache. Write strategies decide what happens when data *changes*. Real systems combine one of each.

## Cache-aside (lazy loading)

This is the most common pattern, and the default for Redis and Memcached. The application talks to both the cache and the database. The cache knows nothing about the database.

```
 read(key):
   1. GET key from cache ---- hit --> return
   2. miss: SELECT from DB
   3. SET key in cache (with TTL)
   4. return value
```

The following uses application-specific database and serialization adapters; it illustrates control flow rather than a complete library integration.

```python
def get_user(user_id):
    key = f"user:{user_id}"
    cached = redis.get(key)
    if cached is not None:
        return deserialise(cached)
    user = db.query(
        "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=%s",
        user_id)
    if user is not None:
        redis.set(key, serialise(user),
                  ex=300)
    return user
```

On a write, the application updates the database and then **deletes** the cache key, so the next read reloads it.

Why delete rather than overwrite with the new value? Deleting is idempotent and cheap, and it avoids two concurrent writers racing to `SET` their versions in the wrong order (the older value could land last and stick). Lesson 4 looks at the races that remain.

**Strengths**

- Only data that is actually requested gets cached, so memory is not wasted.
- With timeouts, fallback and sufficient origin capacity, cache failure can fall back to the database; otherwise the miss surge can overload it.
- Works with any database and any cache.

**Weaknesses**

- The first read of each key is a miss, which costs three trips (cache, DB, cache).
- Cache logic is spread through application code.
- There is a window where the cache and database disagree, and some interleavings of concurrent reads and writes can leave stale data in the cache for a whole TTL (lesson 4).

## Read-through

The cache sits **in line**: the app only talks to the cache, and on a miss the cache itself loads from the database using a loader you configure.

```
 App --> Cache --miss--> DB
     <--       <--------
```

The data flow is the same as cache-aside; the difference is **where the code lives**. Examples include Caffeine's `LoadingCache` in Java, NCache, and DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX), which is a read-through and write-through cache in front of DynamoDB.

Read-through keeps application code simple, and a good library will **coalesce** concurrent misses for the same key into one database query. Note that an in-process library coalesces per process: with 20 app servers, a cold key can still cause up to 20 queries. The cost is coupling: the cache must know how to talk to your database.

## Write-through

On every write, the data is written to the cache **and** to the database synchronously, before the write is acknowledged.

```
 write(key, v):
   App --> Cache --> DB
   ack only after both succeed
```

**Strengths**

- Acknowledging both writes can make read-after-write fresh when ordering and failure handling are correct. Two independent writes alone do not prevent concurrent writers leaving a stale cache value.
- Nothing is lost if the cache crashes, because the database already has it.

**Weaknesses**

- The acknowledgement waits for the required writes; total latency depends on their ordering and possible overlap.
- Data that is written but never read still fills the cache (often fixed by pairing with a TTL).
- If the DB write succeeds and the cache write fails (or the reverse), you need a rule for which one wins. In practice, write to the DB first and treat the cache as best-effort.

## Write-back (write-behind)

Writes go to the cache only, and are acknowledged immediately. The cache flushes them to the database **later**, asynchronously, often in batches.

```
 write --> Cache (ack)
             |  later, batched
             v
             DB
```

This is how CPU caches, the operating system page cache, and database buffer pools work: a "dirty" page is written to disk later.

**Strengths**

- Very low write latency.
- Absorbs bursts and **coalesces** repeated writes. A counter incremented 1,000 times a second can be flushed once a second as a single write.

**Weaknesses**

- **Data loss.** If the cache node dies before flushing, the acknowledged writes are gone, unless the cache itself is durable (replicated, with a write-ahead log).
- The database is behind the cache, so anything reading the database directly (reports, other services) sees old data.
- Ordering and failure handling of the flush are hard to get right.

> [!warning] Write-back changes your source of truth
> With write-back, the cache temporarily *is* the source of truth for recent writes. You need the durability guarantees of a database from it. Use it only where its measured loss window (including delayed or failed flushes) is tolerable (view counters, analytics) or where the cache is genuinely durable.

## Write-around

Writes go **straight to the database**, bypassing the cache. The cache is only filled on reads (usually by cache-aside), and any existing cached copy is invalidated.

This suits data that is written once and rarely read soon afterwards, such as logs, audit records, or uploads. It avoids filling the cache with data nobody asks for. The cost is that a read straight after a write is a miss.

Strictly, "update the DB then delete the key" in cache-aside is write-around plus invalidation, and that is the most common combination in practice.

## Refresh-ahead

A fifth pattern tackles the miss that happens when a popular key expires. With **refresh-ahead**, the cache reloads an entry *before* it expires, once it has been read close to the end of its life. For example, with a 60 s TTL and a refresh factor of 0.8, a read after 48 s returns the current value immediately and triggers a background reload.

- Successful timely refreshes hide expiry for hot keys; slow or failed refreshes can still lead to a miss.
- Keys nobody reads near expiry are left to expire, so cold data is not refreshed for nothing.
- If the predictions are poor, you pay for reloads that nobody uses.

Caffeine's `refreshAfterWrite` is an example. Lesson 7 shows a probabilistic version that also prevents stampedes.

## Comparing them

| Strategy | Write latency | Fresh after write | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Write-through | High (2 writes) | With ordering | Concurrent writes / failures |
| Write-back | Very low | Cache yes, DB no | Data loss on crash |
| Write-around | DB only | Miss on next read | Read-after-write miss |

| Read strategy | Code lives in | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Cache-aside | Application | Simple, resilient, most common |
| Read-through | Cache / library | Cleaner code, can coalesce misses |

## Choosing in practice

1. **Default to cache-aside with delete-on-write and a TTL.** It is a practical default when staleness is acceptable. TTL bounds entry residence rather than source-data age; failures still require safe fallback, origin capacity and reliable refill.
2. Use **read-through** when a library gives it to you cheaply (Caffeine, DAX) and you want built-in miss coalescing.
3. Add **write-through** when reads straight after writes are common and must hit, such as a user editing then viewing their profile.
4. Use **write-back** only for high-volume, loss-tolerant writes, or when the cache layer is designed to be durable.
5. Use **write-around** for write-heavy, read-rarely data.

> [!example] A social feed counter
> Likes on a viral post may arrive at 20,000 per second. A single PostgreSQL row may become a contention bottleneck; benchmark the actual transaction path. Instead, `INCR post:123:likes` in Redis (write-back) and flush the total to Postgres every few seconds. Whether any lost likes are acceptable is a product decision. Restore the baseline from durable state after cache loss and handle flush ordering/idempotency; blindly persisting a reset or old total can lose previously saved counts.

## Key takeaways
- Read strategies: **cache-aside** (app loads on miss) and **read-through** (cache loads on miss).
- Write strategies: **write-through** (cache and DB synchronously), **write-back** (cache now, DB later), **write-around** (DB only).
- Cache-aside with delete-on-write and a TTL is the robust default.
- Write-back gives the lowest latency and coalesces writes, but risks losing acknowledged data.
- Write-through can improve read-after-write freshness when ordering, invalidation and partial failures are handled; it also maintains entries that may never be read.
- Refresh-ahead aims to reload hot keys before expiry, reducing waits when refreshes finish in time.
